(This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: newly introduced(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we right now expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has stated he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing highlighted.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle issues like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: latest(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first problem, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we presently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has mentioned he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing showed.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle complications like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first glitch, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we presently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Sources indicate that for all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing indicated.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle problems like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands.
